description:
🚀 We are Ai Vibecoders

A crew of six space enthusiasts from Dushanbe, Tajikistan. We build things that make space science feel close, hands-on and a little bit fun. This is our second NASA Space Apps Challenge — our 2025 team was named a Global Nominee, and we came back to aim even higher.

👩‍🚀 The crew

Zokirov Dalerjon — team captain

Zokirov Sherzod

Hasanova Mavzuna

Zokirova Mukhiba

Sharipov Mahmudjon

Zokirova Maftuna

🛰️ This year's mission

For the Space Mission Design Game challenge we built Mission Architect — a browser game where you design a spacecraft, choose an orbit and a rocket, fly a year-long mission and get real NASA imagery back. Solo or as a crew of 2–4, every choice costs something elsewhere.

▶ Play it: https://sherzodchat-lang.github.io/mission-architect/

💡 What drives us

We believe the best way to learn how space missions work is to try one — make the trade-offs, watch it fail, understand why, and launch again. We love open data, clean design, games and building fast with modern tools.

Our motto: "We will win!"
summary: Mission Architect is a browser game for the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge. You pick a science goal (Earth CubeSat, Lunar Orbiter or Mars Probe), build a 3D spacecraft from real component classes, and choose orbit, launch vehicle, ground stations and testing while balancing mass, power, budget, data, comms and schedule. Play solo or as a team of 2-4 with mission roles. Then you fly a 12-step mission with solar flares, anomalies and outages, and your spacecraft returns real NASA imagery whose quality depends on your design. A plain-language report explains why the mission worked or failed and names the real NASA mission your design most resembles. It turns abstract engineering trade-offs into something students can try, fail, understand and redesign.
details:
🚀 What it does

Mission Architect is a browser game where you design, fly and debrief a complete space mission. Every choice costs something elsewhere, and there is rarely a single best design — out of about 1.24 million feasible designs, only 0.3–8.8% meet the science goal.

  • Mission — pick a science goal: Earth Observation CubeSat (easy), Lunar Orbiter (medium) or Mars Probe (hard).
  • Design — build a 3D spacecraft from real component classes and watch mass, power, budget, data, comms, schedule (and Δv fuel) update live.
  • Orbit & launch — choose orbit, launch vehicle, ground stations and a test campaign; incompatible choices explain why.
  • Operations — fly 12 steps with solar flares, anomalies, outages and orbit insertion burns, making decisions under pressure.
  • Report — a score, a plain-language "what happened and why" with next time advice, and the real NASA mission your design resembles.

👩‍🚀 Play as a crew (team mode)

2–4 players share one screen as Science Lead, Systems Engineer, Comms & Ground Lead and Mission Manager. Each controls part of the spacecraft and has a personal goal. Turns pass with a "Pass the console" screen, a review board must approve before launch (the Mission Manager has two overrides), flight decisions name their owner, and the report scores Teamwork.

🛰️ Built on real NASA data

  • Your spacecraft returns real NASA imagery — live NASA GIBS (MODIS), Moon Trek and Mars Trek frames that are sharp, blurred, cut or noisy depending on your pointing, downlink, storage, radiation and orbit.
  • NASA GMAT R2026a — 14 orbit runs give sunlight fraction, eclipse length, ground-station contact time and LEO lifetime.
  • JPL Horizons — real Earth–Mars signal delay and Earth–Moon distance; Mars launch windows computed from Horizons planet positions.
  • NASA Small Spacecraft Technology State of the Art 2025 and CubeSat 101 — component values backed by 105 page-cited quotes.
  • 23 real analog missions matched to your design, with NSSDCA facts, NASA Image and Video Library photos and NTRS papers.
  • Photoreal Earth, Moon and Mars from Blue Marble, Black Marble, LRO and Viking/MGS imagery — 33 NASA and partner sources listed in-game.

🎯 Benefits and impact

Students rarely get to try a whole mission from concept to operation. Mission Architect makes the trade-offs tangible: every warning says what happened, why, and what to change, and the redesign-and-relaunch loop turns failure into learning. It is free, runs in any desktop browser, needs no install, and is open source.

For judges: open the project link with ?demo=1 for a ready design, then use 4× speed and "Skip to end".

🛠️ How we built it

  • Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand; three.js / react-three-fiber for procedural 3D spacecraft and planets; Howler.js audio.
  • A deterministic TypeScript engine with 100+ automated tests (Vitest) and a Python balance checker over every possible design.
  • Python and Node data tools for GMAT scripts and the Horizons and NTRS snapshots; deployed on GitHub Pages.
  • Source code (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/sherzodchat-lang/mission-architect

🤖 Use of SI and credits

Code was written with an SI coding agent (Anthropic Claude Code) under the team's direction and review; the game concept, rules and design were defined by the team. Voice lines, sound effects and narration were generated with ElevenLabs and acknowledged in file metadata. Card art was generated with OpenAI image generation and carries a visible "SI-generated" label in the game. No NASA logos or branding were used. Mission Architect is an educational simulation and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

🔭 What's next

  • More missions (asteroids, Venus, Europa, the Sun), online multiplayer and classroom lesson plans.
